https://13wham.com/news/local/rabid-racc.text: Warsaw, N.Y. — A raccoon has tested positive for rabies after two people reported separate encounters with raccoons in the village of Warsaw, according to the Wyoming County Department of Health. The two people are receiving rabies post-exposure treatment following the incidents. Laboratory testing confirmed one of the raccoons had the disease. The health department also received a report Thursday from Warsaw police about another raccoon showing signs of illness. Wyoming County officials are urging people to avoid wildlife, particularly animals displaying unusual or aggressive behavior. Pets should also be kept away from wild animals and remain up to date on their rabies vaccinations. Anyone bitten or scratched by an animal that may have rabies should immediately wash the wound with soap and water and contact a health care provider and the county health department. The Warsaw case comes amid recent rabies cases in neighboring Livingston County, where two cows on the same farm tested positive this week. Two exposed farmers are receiving preventative treatment. MORE: 2 rabid cows found in Livingston County; 2 farmers exposed Wyoming County's next free rabies vaccination clinic for dogs, cats and ferrets is scheduled for Nov. 7 from 9 to 11 a.m. at the Wyoming County Highway Department.

https://www.americamagazine.org/vatican-.text: Sections Politics Faith Culture Vatican Scripture Podcasts More from America Podcasts Video Newsletters Events Voices YouTube Mobile App About Us Careers Contact Us Print Edition November 2026 Past Issues November 2026 Current Issue Facebook X YouTube Instagram Sections Politics Faith Culture Vatican Scripture Podcasts More from America Podcasts Video Newsletters Events Voices YouTube Mobile App About Us Careers Contact Us Print Edition November 2026 Past Issues November 2026 Current Issue Facebook X YouTube Instagram Pope Leo XIV greets a baby and family at the conclusion of his weekly general audience in the Paul VI Audience Hall at the Vatican Aug. 27, 2025. Credit: CNS photo/Vatican Media The Vatican today released a detailed program for the week-long meeting (Oct. 7-14) of the presidents of the world’s 115 Catholic bishops’ conferences and the heads of the 21 Eastern churches, convened by Pope Leo XIV, 10 years after the publication of Pope Francis’ post-synodal exhortation on the family, “ Amoris Laetitia ” (“The Joy of Love”). Announcing the meeting on March 19 , the American-born pope asked the bishops to discern with him the steps needed “in order to proclaim the Gospel to families today, in light of Amoris Laetitia and taking into account what is currently being done in the local churches.” “Our era is marked by rapid changes which make it necessary, even more than ten years ago, to give particular pastoral attention to families, to whom the Lord entrusts the task of participating in the Church’s mission of proclaiming and witnessing to the Gospel,” the pope said then. [Top 10 takeaways from “Amoris Laetitia”] Detailed information about this event, including the list of participants, was given at today’s Vatican press conference by Gabriela Gambino, the undersecretary of the Dicastery for the Laity, Family and Life; Orietta Rachele Grazioli, who teaches canon and comparative law of the family at the Pontifical John Paul II Institute for the Sciences of Marriage and the Family in Rome; and Giacomo Costa, S.J., consultor of the General Secretary of the Synod, who is responsible for the methodology of next week’s encounter. Pope Leo and the various presenters have alluded to the many social, political and cultural changes that have happened since Pope Francis published “Amoris Laetitia” on March 19, 2016, impacting families worldwide. Among the primary challenges are the Covid-19 pandemic; the wars in Ukraine, Gaza and the Holy Land, Lebanon, Iran, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Sudan; the migration crisis; the Trump presidency; the rise of A.I. ; growing inequality in the world; climate change; growing secularization in many places; religious persecution; and the decrease of vocations in the Western world. Many bishops who will be in attendance come from very difficult situations. Some 248 bishops, five families representing each of the continents and a number of experts will participate in the meeting, Ms. Gambino said. The list published by the Vatican shows that, in addition to the presidents of the bishops’ conferences and the heads of the Oriental churches, Pope Leo has appointed 22 other cardinals and bishops to participate in the meeting. They include four Americans: Cardinals Blase Cupich, Robert McElroy and Joseph Tobin and Bishop Daniel Flores. Noteworthy among the other cardinals are Luis Antonio Tagle and Victor Manuel Fernandez (Vatican), Gerald Lacroix (Quebec), Jean-Claude Hollerich (Luxembourg), José Cobo Cano (Madrid), Pablo Virgilio David (Philippines), Protase Rugambwa (Tanzania) and Dogbo Ignace Bessi (Ivory Coast), as well as Bishop Joseph Dabrowski (Canada) and two bishops from mainland China: Joseph Huang Binghang and Matteo Zhen Xuebin. The meeting will take place behind closed doors. Ms. Gambino recalled that Pope Leo called this meeting for bishops to listen to each other and summarize what has happened in their local churches during the 10 years since “Amoris Laetitia,” a text that “has oriented” their conferences’ work in a decade that has seen “rapid cultural and social transformations,” with differing pastoral realities in the different continents. The pope then wants the bishops to “discern together” what steps the Spirit is calling them to take in the years ahead to proclaim the Gospel to and with families. During their five-yearly “ad limina” visits to the Holy See, she said, bishops “had expressed concern” about the difficulties they encountered in their pastoral ministry to families, the challenges families face in their daily lives and in the transmission of the faith. She noted, for example, that in Poland, marriages celebrated in church have decreased by 45 percent over the last five years, while in Australia, between 1970 and 2024, the number of church marriages decreased from 88 to 16 percent. She said the basic question facing this meeting is “how to renew with vigor the pastoral [ministry] and make families participate ever more in the life and mission of the church.” Ms. Grazioli said the 10th anniversary of “Amoris Laetitia” was “an opportune” moment to see “the pastoral creativity born from the full text of ‘Amoris Laetitia,’ obviously in different ways in the different regions of the world.” She said “listen and discern” are two key words for this meeting as the bishops focus on the five main themes: “Families today: reality, beauty, challenges”; “Young people and the discovery of the vocation to marriage”; “Married life. The first years of marriage: a decisive time”; “In the difficulties of life: accompanying and supporting”; and “Christian families as subjects of the church’s mission.” In his presentation, Father Costa said this meeting could be considered as “a kind of evaluation” assembly. He explained that “evaluation does not mean passing judgment on the text—whether to praise or criticize it—but rather learning from the experience gained since its publication, in order to recognize where the Holy Spirit is leading the church and what new steps He is asking us to take.” In the light of this understanding, Father Costa offered a clear explanation of what this meeting is aiming at: Ten years after the publication of “Amoris Laetitia”… it is not primarily a matter of commenting on the exhortation once again, but of re-examining a story: what ‘Amoris Laetitia’ has set in motion in the lives of the churches and families, what we have learned, the difficulties we have encountered, and the new questions that have arisen. Telling this story is already a way of understanding it: through the narrative, transformations, fruits, and questions emerge that a simple assessment of the text’s application might fail to see. Ten years later, the question is not what ‘Amoris Laetitia’ says, but what we have learned by trying to live it out. He said that “the goal set forth by Pope Leo XIV is to proceed, through mutual listening, to a synodal discernment of the steps to be taken today to proclaim the Gospel with families.” Methodology Father Costa said the bishops and experts will share their diverse experiences and perspectives, and most of the time will be spent in the working groups, where they will use the “ conversations in the Spirit ” method, “alternating between speaking, listening and silence.” Through three rounds in the groups, he said, “sharing each person’s experience, reflecting on what has been heard from others and jointly processing what has emerged—participants will seek to highlight points of convergence, as well as differences, tensions, open questions and possible steps to take. We will not seek to erase differences in order to reach a consensus: Even a better-understood divergence can be a fruit of listening. Each group will offer a brief report to the assembly, which will be taken up and explored further in the plenary dialogue.” He said “the fruits of the five days” of work will be compiled into a synthesis report. He emphasized that “this is not a new final document replacing the apostolic exhortation but a summary of what the assembly has recognized through listening and discernment.” A commission, he said, which will include representatives of the assembly, “will verify that the text faithfully reflects what has emerged; the summary will then be discussed by the assembly itself before being entrusted to the Holy Father.” It is not clear what Pope Leo will do with it. The bishops will take it back to their conferences or churches to open whatever new ways ahead are proposed. Press briefings will be held during the week, and the synthesis report will be made public. It should be underlined that the meeting is a joint venture of the Dicastery for the Laity, Family and Life headed by the Irish American cardinal Kevin Farrell and the General Secretariat for the Synod led by the Maltese cardinal Mario Grech. Pope Leo will give an opening address on the afternoon of the first day, Oct. 7, and Helen Alford, O.P., the president of the Pontifical Academy of Social Sciences, will offer a meditation to the assembly. Pope Leo is expected to attend the plenary sessions and will celebrate Mass in St. Peter’s Square on the morning of the closing day, Wednesday, Oct. 14. Photograph: Madison Swart/AP US midterm elections 2026 Outrage after Meta suspends No Kings Instagram account during protests ‘Meta owes us an explanation,’ group says as organizers fear censorship after account goes dark for several hours Sanya Mansoor Sun 18 Oct 2026 20.00 BST Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 20.01 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The coalition leaders behind nationwide pro-democracy protests that have drawn millions of Americans to the streets in recent years were frustrated when its Instagram account was temporarily shut down during its latest demonstration on Saturday . The No Kings movement’s account went dark for several hours while protests focused on increasing early voter turnout were underway, sparking censorship fears. Meta apologized on Saturday and blamed the account’s temporary suspension on an automated action that’s triggered “when accounts post, share or comment at very high frequencies”. “Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone, wrote on X . “Everything is now working as it should and we sincerely apologize.” “We have regained access to our accounts, but Meta still owes us an explanation,” the No Kings Coalition posted on their Instagram page , on Sunday. “Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.” Organizers remained skeptical about Meta’s explanation that high-frequency posting triggered an automated response, and said members “posted only a handful of times and livestreamed to thousands”. Senator Bernie Sanders also expressed concerns on Sunday , on X, saying that “billionaire ownership of the media” had resulted in the suspension of the No Kings account. Despite the technical blip, hundreds of planned events continued . At the Lincoln Memorial in Washington , a band played for a few hundred people in caps and coats, many of whom were dancing and held signs saying “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!” In Atlanta , city councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd: “The constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?” On the streets of downtown Los Angeles, protesters carried umbrellas to protect them from the sweltering heat and a band trailed behind them on a rolling stage, the New York Times reported ; the crowds cheered calls for abolishing ICE and passing California’s billionaire tax. The No Kings movement began last summer, in response to a broad set of concerns about federal layoffs, immigration enforcement and foreign wars. The demonstrations have continued to tackle a wide range of issues, and typically lean into anti-Trump fervor. This year’s focus on voting ahead of the midterm elections is in part due to the supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, as well as fears about Trump once again sowing chaos by baselessly calling election results into question . No Kings organizers said they planned to recruit volunteers at Saturday’s events to mobilize in case of “election sabotage”, Leah Greenberg, a co-executive director of Indivisible, a progressive group that helps organize No Kings events, previously told the Guardian .
